title: Just sitting
hookLine: Dogen: just sit; sitting itself is awakening
carry: like a car passing outside the window

cards: A young monk comes home to Japan from China, and people want to know what he brought back. Scrolls? Statues?
Relics? In a talk recorded years later, Dogen says he came home empty-handed. All he brought back, he said, was that the eyes are horizontal and the nose is vertical.
It sounds like a joke, and maybe it is. But it points at what he taught for the rest of his life: nothing extra, no treasure hidden somewhere else. Just this face, this body, this cushion.

teach.b: The word is shikantaza, a Japanese term usually rendered just sitting, or nothing but sitting. In a short text on how to sit, Dogen keeps it plain.
Find a quiet room. Sit on a thick cushion, upright, leaning neither left nor right, forward nor back. Breathe quietly.
Then let go of the whole wheel of thinking: don't judge thoughts good or bad, don't chase them, don't push them away. Here's the turn.
For Dogen, this sitting is not a ladder you climb to reach awakening somewhere above it.
Practice and awakening are not two things. You don't sit to get enlightened later, the way you'd save money for a car. The sitting itself is awakening, showing up right now in a body on a cushion.
So nothing gets added: no counting, no picture, no question to solve, no goal held out in front. Dogen also passes on an old exchange. A monk asks a teacher what he thinks about, sitting so still.
The teacher says he thinks of not-thinking.
How do you think of not-thinking? Non-thinking. Thoughts arrive and leave, and nobody grabs them.
Soto Zen, which looks back to Dogen, keeps this sitting at its center. It's the difference between waiting for a bus and simply sitting at the bus stop.

how: In Soto Zen temples and sitting groups, people sit zazen facing a wall or the room, upright on a cushion, without counting the breath or working on a koan, and some groups recite Dogen's instructions on sitting together.

games.q: people ask the young monk home from China what treasures he brought back. what does he say?
o: a cart of scrolls and statues
nothing: eyes are horizontal, the nose is vertical
a secret method for quick awakening
games.why: in a recorded talk, Dogen says he came home empty-handed, with only the plain fact of his own face.

practice: Sit upright the way Dogen describes, not stiff, not slumped, hands resting, and let the breath breathe itself without counting it.
When a thought arrives, a plan, a worry, a song, let it come and go like a car passing outside the window; if you notice you've followed one down the street, that noticing is fine too.
Come back to just this body, sitting here, with nothing to get and nothing to fix.

wordCard.voice: Shikantaza. Just sitting, nothing added, which Dogen taught is awakening itself rather than a road toward it. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese shikantaza: just sitting, nothing but sitting, Dogen's word for zazen.

carryVoice: Your line: like a car passing outside the window. You don't have to chase a single one. Day nine hundred ninety-seven, done.

sources.ref: Shobogenzo, Zazenshin (the Yaoshan exchange on not-thinking)
